In a few spots, ordering strictly by atomic weight put an element in the wrong chemical family. The weights said one order, but the chemistry clearly demanded another. The most famous case, by weight, tellurium and iodine fall in one order, but their chemical behavior insisted on the reverse. For decades, those swaps looked like blemishes, little inconsistencies. The resolution came only in 1913 from a young physicist named Henry Moseley, who was probing atoms with X-rays. Moseley found that the true thing that orders the elements is not their weight at all. It's a whole number he could measure, which we now call the atomic number.

The number of protons in the nucleus, the count of positive charges at the atom's core. And when you order the elements by atomic number, instead of atomic weight, every one of Mendeleev's troublesome swaps clicks into place automatically. Tellurium really does come before iodine by atomic number, even though it's heavier.

Mendeleev had been right to trust the chemistry because the chemistry was secretly tracking atomic number, the real quantity, while atomic weight was just a usually reliable stand-in for it. He'd been reading the correct order off the behavior without knowing what the correct order actually counted. But why was atomic weight ever out of step with atomic number in the first place?

Most of the time, they rise together. What makes them occasionally disagree? Because atomic weight is an average, and averages can be lumpy. Here's the thing nobody knew in Mendeleev's day. It turns out most elements aren't made of identical atoms. They're a mixture of isotopes, atoms with the same number of protons, so the same atomic number and the same chemistry, but different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different weights.

Chlorine, for instance, is a blend of a lighter and a heavier kind of chlorine atom. The atomic weight you measure is the average over that mixture, weighted by how common each isotope is. So the weight of an element depends not just on its proton count, but on the accident of which isotopes it happens to have, and in what proportions.

And that's exactly how an element like tellurium can end up heavier than iodine, even though it has fewer protons. Tellurium simply happens to carry more heavy isotopes. Atomic number, the proton count, is a clean whole number identity that never lies. Atomic weight is a slightly lumpy average that usually tracks it, but occasionally stumbles.
Mendeleev caught those stumbles purely by chemical instinct, swapping the elements to where their behavior said they belonged.
